title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
description: Turn users into requests, bytes, and machines with round numbers you can do in your head.

lessons.title: Numbers to keep in your head
lessons.summary: Powers of two, byte units, seconds per day, and the sizes of everyday data.

steps.prompt: Roughly how many bytes is 2^30 bytes?
steps.why: Every factor of 2^10 (1,024) is about ×1,000, so 2^30 = (2^10)^3 ≈ 1,000^3 = 1 billion. The exact value is 1,073,741,824.

misconceptions.About 1 million (1 MB): That's 2^20. Each extra 10 in the exponent adds three zeros: 2^10 ≈ 10^3, 2^20 ≈ 10^6, 2^30 ≈ 10^9.
misconceptions.About 1 trillion (1 TB): That's 2^40, one step of 2^10 too far.
misconceptions.About 30 thousand: The exponent counts doublings: 2 multiplied by itself 30 times, not 30 × 1,000.

steps.title: Powers of two ≈ powers of ten
steps.body: 2^10 is 1,024: close enough to 1,000. So every +10 in the exponent adds three zeros, and 2^30 bytes ≈ 1 billion bytes ≈ 1 GB. The error stays under ~13% all the way to petabytes, which is far below the precision of an estimate.

steps.prompt: Match each unit to its size in bytes (estimate-level precision).
steps.why: Each unit is 1,000× the one before, so moving one rung changes the exponent by 3. That's what lets you convert 5 × 10^12 bytes to 5 TB at a glance.

steps.title: A day is about 100K seconds
steps.body: A day has 86,400 seconds. Round it to **100K** and turning a daily total into a per-second rate is just dropping five zeros. The rounding makes rates about 14% low, which is noise next to the 2–3× peak factor you'll apply later.

steps.text: Dividing by 100K seconds: 1 billion requests a day is about [[10K]] per second, and 50 million a day is about [[500]] per second. Going the other way, 2,000 requests per second is about [[200M]] a day.
steps.why: Per day → per second divides by 10^5; per second → per day multiplies by 10^5. 1B ÷ 100K = 10K, 50M ÷ 100K = 500, and 2,000 × 100K = 200M.

steps.title: Sizes of everyday data
steps.body: Most estimates multiply a count by a size, so memorize a few anchors. They're rough: real rows add indexes and overhead, and media size depends heavily on resolution and compression. Text is bytes, photos are hundreds of KB, video is tens of MB per minute.

steps.prompt: Which size range does each item fall into?

items.why: 128 bits = 16 bytes in binary (36 bytes as a text string).

items.text: A short text post with its metadata
items.why: ~300 bytes: text plus IDs, timestamps, and counters.
A small JPEG is a few KB.

items.text: A photo as stored by a social app (compressed)
items.why: Resized and recompressed photos are typically a few hundred KB.

steps.why: Text lives in bytes, images in kilobytes, and audio and video in megabytes and up. Knowing the bucket tells you which data dominates storage.

steps.prompt: An analytics pipeline stores 1 billion click events, each just a user ID and a timestamp. How much raw storage is that?
steps.hint: A billion of anything that's N bytes is N GB.
steps.why: A billion records of N bytes is N GB, so no conversion is needed. A real database adds per-row headers and indexes, which can easily double or triple a row this small.

steps.prompt: How many compressed photos fit on a 1 TB disk?
steps.hint: TB ÷ KB is 10^12 ÷ 10^3 = 10^9. Then divide by 500.
steps.why: Split the problem into exponents and leading digits: TB ÷ KB = 10^9, and 10^9 ÷ 500 = 2 × 10^6. Keeping the exponents separate is how you avoid being off by 1,000×.

lessons.title: From users to QPS
lessons.summary: Daily users × actions ÷ 100K seconds = average QPS, then peaks and the read/write split.

steps.prompt: A note-taking app has 10M daily active users, each making about 10 requests a day. What's the average load?
steps.why: 10M × 10 = 100M requests a day, and 100M ÷ 100K seconds ≈ 1,000 requests/sec.

misconceptions.~100,000 requests/sec: That divides by 1,000 instead of by the ~100K seconds in a day.
misconceptions.~10,000 requests/sec: Off by 10×: 100M ÷ 100K is 1,000. Count the zeros: 10^8 ÷ 10^5 = 10^3.
misconceptions.~100 requests/sec: That divides by 1M seconds; a day is only ~100K seconds.

steps.title: The QPS formula
steps.body: **Average QPS = DAU × actions per user per day ÷ 100K seconds.** Count only actions that hit your servers, and treat reads and writes separately when they differ. Write the daily total down: it feeds the storage estimate too. This gives the average; capacity is sized for the peak.

steps.prompt: A messaging app: how many messages are sent per second, on average?
given: Messages sent per user per day
steps.why: Multiply to a daily total first, then divide once by 100K. Doing it in that order keeps the zeros easy to track and gives you the daily volume for later storage math.

steps.title: Size for the peak
steps.body: Traffic isn't flat: people use apps in the evening, not at 4 a.m. A typical daily peak is **2–3× the average**; launches, flash sales, and live events can spike **10× or more**. Servers sized for the average fall over every evening, so size for the peak.

steps.prompt: A ride-hailing app: what peak QPS must the API handle?
given: API calls per user per day
steps.why: Peak, not average, decides how many servers you need. The average (5K/sec) is a stepping stone; the design number is 15K/sec.

steps.context: A concert-ticket site averages 1K requests/sec across the day. Tickets for a stadium tour go on sale at 10:00 sharp.
steps.prompt: Which peak assumption is most defensible for sale time?
options: 10× or more: demand piles into a few minutes
steps.answer: 10× or more: demand piles into a few minutes
steps.why: When everyone arrives at the same instant, a day's demand lands in minutes and peak-to-average can reach 10–100×. That's why ticket sites put buyers in virtual waiting rooms.

misconceptions.2–3×: the usual daily peak: That rule of thumb is for smooth daily cycles. An on-sale moment concentrates demand far more sharply.
misconceptions.1×: design for the average: The average hides the spike; the site would go down exactly when it matters most.

steps.prompt: Fitness trackers upload a reading every 5 minutes, day and night. What's the average upload rate?
solution: Cross-check: 5M devices ÷ 300 s between uploads ≈ 17K/sec, same ballpark
steps.why: Devices on a timer produce flat traffic, so here peak ≈ average, unlike human traffic. The real danger is all devices reconnecting at once after an outage, which is why device schedules get random jitter.

steps.title: Reads vs writes
steps.body: Most user-facing systems are **read-heavy**: a post is written once and read many times. Estimate write QPS from user actions, then multiply by the **read:write ratio** for read QPS. Reads drive caches and replicas; writes drive database write capacity and sharding.

steps.prompt: A URL shortener: what's the average redirect (read) QPS?
steps.why: Get write QPS from the stated volume, then scale by the ratio. Using 86,400 s instead gives ≈1,160 writes and ≈11,600 reads per second, the same answer within rounding.

steps.text: Average QPS = [[DAU]] × [[actions per user per day]] ÷ [[100K]] seconds. To size servers, multiply by a [[peak factor]]; to get read QPS from write QPS, multiply by the [[read:write ratio]].
steps.why: Daily users and their actions give the daily volume, and 100K s turns it into a rate. Peak factor and read:write ratio adjust that rate; MAU overstates daily traffic, and replication factor belongs to storage, not traffic.

lessons.title: Storage and bandwidth
lessons.summary: Record size × volume × retention × replicas, and QPS × payload for the network.

steps.prompt: A photo app stores 10M new photos a day at ~500 KB each and keeps them for 5 years. Roughly how much raw storage is that, before replication?
steps.why: 10M × 500 KB = 5 TB per day. Five years is ~1,800 days, and 5 TB × 1,800 = 9,000 TB ≈ 9 PB.

misconceptions.~9 TB: That's under two days of uploads: 10M × 500 KB is already 5 TB per day.
misconceptions.~90 TB: That's about 18 days of uploads. Five years is ~1,800 days, 100× more.
misconceptions.~900 PB: 100× too big. Check the conversion: 500 KB × 10M = 5 × 10^12 bytes = 5 TB per day.

steps.title: The storage formula
steps.body: **Storage = record size × records per day × days retained × replication factor.** Three copies is a common default for durability. Worked: 10M photos × 500 KB = 5 TB/day; × 1,800 days (5 years) ≈ 9 PB; × 3 replicas ≈ 27 PB. Say which factors you include.

steps.prompt: A microblogging service: how much storage for one year of posts, including replicas?
steps.why: Text is small: hundreds of millions of posts a day is still only TB-scale per year. Media attachments, not text, push storage into petabytes.

steps.prompt: A video platform: how much new storage does it need per day for the original uploads (one copy)?
steps.why: Video dwarfs everything else. Real platforms then transcode each upload into several resolutions and replicate them, multiplying this number again.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a storage estimate in order.
items: State assumptions: users, uploads per user, bytes per upload
Uploads per day = users × uploads per user
Bytes per day = uploads per day × bytes per upload
Total = bytes per day × days retained × replication factor
Sanity-check: how many disks or machines is that?
steps.why: Each step uses the result of the one before, so this order keeps the arithmetic checkable. The final sanity check translates the total into hardware, where unit slips become obvious.

steps.title: Bandwidth
steps.body: **Bandwidth = requests per second × bytes per request**, or daily bytes ÷ 100K s. Ingress comes from writes (uploads), egress from reads (downloads), and egress dominates read-heavy apps. Network links are rated in **bits**, so multiply bytes by 8.

steps.prompt: An image service's origin servers handle every image read. What's the egress bandwidth?
steps.why: Egress dominates read-heavy media apps. Serving 32 Gbps from origin is why images go behind a CDN, which absorbs most reads close to users.

steps.prompt: Peak egress is 250 MB/s. What does that require from the network, in bits?
steps.why: Storage is quoted in bytes, networks in bits: 250 MB/s × 8 = 2,000 Mbps ≈ 2 Gbps.

misconceptions.250 Mbps: MB (bytes) and Mb (bits) differ by 8×. Mixing them is the most common bandwidth mistake.
misconceptions.~31 Mbps: That divides by 8. A byte is 8 bits, so the bit rate is the bigger number.
misconceptions.~20 Gbps: That multiplies by 80. One byte is 8 bits, so it's 250 × 8 = 2,000 Mbps.

steps.prompt: A document-scanning app: what's the average upload (ingress) bandwidth?
steps.why: Daily volume ÷ 100K s gives the average rate. Provision links for the peak (2–3× this) and convert to bits (× 8) before comparing with link speeds.

lessons.title: Servers, caches, and sanity checks
lessons.summary: Turn QPS and bytes into machines, size a cache with the 80/20 rule, and catch absurd results.

steps.prompt: For a first estimate, about how many simple API requests per second can one commodity app server handle?
steps.why: A server doing a quick lookup, some JSON, and a cache or database call per request handles thousands per second. It's an assumption, so say it out loud, and go lower for heavy requests like search or image processing.

misconceptions.~10: That's a very heavy request, such as rendering a video thumbnail. Simple API calls are hundreds of times cheaper.
misconceptions.~1M: Highly tuned proxies or in-memory stores can approach that, but app servers doing real work (auth, serialization, database calls) handle thousands.
misconceptions.~100M: That's more than the total traffic of most large services; no single machine comes close.

steps.title: How many servers?
steps.body: **Servers = peak QPS ÷ QPS per server.** State the per-server number as an assumption: it varies 100× with request cost. Then add headroom: run at ~70% utilization so a spike or a lost machine doesn't tip you over, and keep at least one spare (N+1).

steps.prompt: A search API: how many servers does the peak load need, before headroom and spares?
given: 500 searches/sec (search is heavier than a simple call)
steps.why: Chain the steps: daily volume, average, peak, then divide by per-server capacity. With ~70% utilization and a spare you'd deploy about 12 ÷ 0.7 + 1 ≈ 18.

steps.title: Sizing a cache with 80/20
steps.body: Reads are skewed: roughly **20% of items get 80% of reads** (a heuristic, not a law). So cache the hot 20%: **cache size ≈ 20% × daily reads × item size**. That's an upper bound, since hot items repeat. Then divide by usable RAM per node to count cache machines.

items.label: RAM on a typical cache node

steps.prompt: A URL shortener caches hot redirects. Using the 80/20 rule, how much cache memory does it need?
given: Share of daily reads to cache
steps.why: 100 GB fits in the RAM of one or two machines, which is why caching a URL shortener is cheap. Because hot keys repeat, the real working set is smaller still.

steps.prompt: A social app's profile cache works out to 2 TB. How many cache nodes does it need, before replicas?
given: ≈ 100 GB per node (the rest goes to the OS and overhead)
steps.why: Divide by usable memory, not the number on the box. If losing a node shouldn't flood the database with misses, add replicas (often ×2).

steps.title: Sanity-check every answer
steps.body: Before trusting a number, hold it against reality. Is 1 PB of RAM plausible? At 256 GB per machine, that's ~4,000 servers just for cache: a red flag. Recheck units (bits vs bytes, KB vs MB), since one slip is a 1,000× error, and compare with systems you know.

rows: 100 GB cache for a URL shortener
1 PB of RAM for a cache

steps.context: Your cache estimate for a photo-sharing app comes out at 1 PB of RAM.
steps.prompt: What's the best next move?
options: Recheck assumptions: you're probably caching full images or all data instead of hot metadata
Move the cache onto spinning disks to save money
Drop the cache; the database can serve everything
steps.answer: Recheck assumptions: you're probably caching full images or all data instead of hot metadata
steps.why: An absurd total usually means a modeling error. Image bytes belong in object storage behind a CDN; the in-memory cache holds small, hot metadata, typically GBs to low TBs.

misconceptions.Order ~4,000 large-memory servers: Possible in principle, but a wild number is far more often a mistake. Fix the model before buying hardware.
misconceptions.Move the cache onto spinning disks to sa: A disk-backed cache throws away the point of caching: memory-speed reads. Large blobs go to a CDN.
misconceptions.Drop the cache; the database can serve e: The read load that made you want a cache doesn't go away; the database would take all of it.

steps.prompt: Explain how you'd size the cache for a read-heavy service. Which numbers do you need, and how do you combine them?

concepts.label: Start from the read volume (read QPS or reads per day)
Multiply by the size of each cached item
Divide by usable memory per machine to get a node count

steps.model: Start from the read volume: read QPS × 100K seconds gives reads per day. Apply the 80/20 rule and cache the hot 20% of those reads, multiplied by the object size, e.g. 1B reads/day × 20% × 500 bytes = 100 GB. Finally divide by usable memory per machine to get the number of cache nodes, and add replicas for failover.
steps.why: Cache size is a chain of three numbers (how much is read, how much of it is hot, how big each item is) followed by a hardware check. Stating each one lets an interviewer correct a single link without redoing the rest.
